cards.front: Otto Loewi stimulated the vagus nerve of one isolated frog heart, which slows its beat, then moved fluid that had bathed it onto a second heart whose own vagus was untouched. The second heart slowed too. What did this show?
cards.back: The nerve had acted by releasing a chemical into the fluid, later identified as acetylcholine. A nerve's message at its target can be chemical.
cards.quote: The nerve had acted by releasing a chemical, later identified as acetylcholine.

cards.front: A drug's {{c1::target}} is the protein it binds, such as a receptor, a transporter or an enzyme.
cards.quote: a drug's target is the protein it binds, such as a receptor, a transporter or an enzyme.
cards.section: A chemical message and three puzzles

cards.front: By what one rule do you classify a drug acting on a transmitter system, and what sets the size of its effect?
cards.back: Classify it by the main step it changes: release, reading (receptors) or removal. The size depends on how much of its target it fills.
cards.quote: Classify a drug by the main step of a transmitter system it changes: release, reading or removal.
cards.section: A chemical message and three puzzles

cards.front: What three steps does every transmitter's signal go through, and what are the three parts of a transmitter system called?
cards.back: It is released, read and removed. The parts are the source (neurons that release it), the readers (receptors) and the off switch (what clears it).
cards.quote: Source, readers, off switch: together they make a transmitter system.
cards.section: The idea: three steps, and a drug changes mainly one

cards.front: How do ionotropic and metabotropic receptors differ in how they work and how fast they act?
cards.back: An ionotropic receptor is itself an ion channel: binding opens it and current flows within milliseconds. A metabotropic receptor is a GPCR with no pore; it starts a messenger chain, so effects take tens of milliseconds to minutes.
cards.quote: It starts a chain of messengers inside the cell, so its effects take tens of milliseconds to minutes.
cards.section: The idea: three steps, and a drug changes mainly one

cards.front: In the lock-and-key picture of a synapse, a drug that fits the receptor but will not turn it, so the real key cannot get in, is a {{c1::competitive antagonist}}.
cards.quote: a key that fits but will not turn, so the real key cannot get in: a competitive antagonist
cards.section: The idea: three steps, and a drug changes mainly one

cards.front: What is a positive allosteric modulator?
cards.back: A drug that binds a site other than the transmitter's own and makes the transmitter's effect stronger: oil in the lock, so the real key turns more easily.
cards.quote: oil in the lock, so the real key turns more easily: a positive allosteric modulator (allosteric means acting from another site)
cards.section: The idea: three steps, and a drug changes mainly one

cards.front: At a mature synapse where GABA inhibits, four drugs are tested. Baclofen activates GABA-B receptors. Bicuculline sits in the GABA site of GABA-A receptors without opening them. Diazepam binds another site on GABA-A receptors and strengthens GABA's effect. Tiagabine blocks GAT1, a transporter that clears GABA. Which strengthen inhibition, and which weaken it?
cards.back: Baclofen, diazepam and tiagabine strengthen inhibition. Bicuculline weakens it; in animals it causes seizures.
cards.why: Baclofen fakes the signal at one reader, diazepam strengthens it at another, tiagabine keeps GABA around longer, and bicuculline blocks the reader. The step changed, and its direction, decide the effect.
cards.quote: What decides the effect is which step a drug changes, and in which direction.
cards.section: The idea: three steps, and a drug changes mainly one

cards.front: What decides whether a transmitter excites or inhibits a cell?
cards.back: Not the transmitter itself but the receptor and the ion gradient. An open channel pulls Vm toward that ion's equilibrium potential, so where that potential sits relative to Vm and threshold sets the sign.
cards.quote: A transmitter is not excitatory or inhibitory by nature. The receptor and the ion gradient decide.

cards.front: A neuron rests at −70 mV with threshold at −50 mV, and its E_Cl is −56 mV. GABA opens GABA-A channels (treated as chloride channels), the chloride conductance equals the resting conductance, and there is no other input. Where does Vm settle, and does GABA fire the cell?
cards.back: Vm settles halfway: (−70 + −56)/2 = −63 mV. That is a depolarization, but it stays below the −50 mV threshold, so GABA does not fire the cell; it opposes excitation that pushes Vm past −56 mV.
cards.quote: With the chloride and resting conductances equal and no other input, Vm settles at the balance point, halfway

cards.front: When E_Cl lies between rest and threshold, GABA depolarizes the cell slightly. Why can it still oppose excitation (shunting)?
cards.back: Any excitation that pushes Vm past E_Cl meets an opposing chloride current through the open GABA-A channels, so GABA usually blunts excitation arriving at the same time.
cards.quote: so GABA usually blunts excitation that arrives at the same time, an effect called shunting

cards.front: GABA opens GABA-A channels in an immature neuron whose E_Cl is −45 mV, above its threshold. What does GABA do, and why?
cards.back: It can excite the cell: the channels pull Vm up toward −45 mV, which lies past threshold.
cards.why: The receptor is the same one that usually inhibits in mature neurons, where E_Cl sits near or below rest. The chloride gradient decides the sign.
cards.quote: Same transmitter, same receptor; the chloride gradient decided the sign.

cards.front: In an immature neuron whose E_Cl is −45 mV, above threshold, GABA can excite. Predict how diazepam changes GABA's action in this neuron.
cards.back: Diazepam should strengthen GABA's excitatory effect, because it increases the GABA-A current, which here pulls Vm toward −45 mV, past threshold.
cards.why: A positive allosteric modulator boosts the reader's effect; the chloride gradient, not the drug, sets the sign of that effect.
cards.quote: Where E_Cl sits on it sets what GABA does.

cards.front: What is the brain's main excitatory transmitter, and what are its three ionotropic receptors?
cards.back: Glutamate. Its ionotropic receptors are AMPA, kainate and NMDA; it also acts at metabotropic glutamate receptors.
cards.quote: Three ionotropic receptors (AMPA, kainate and NMDA) and metabotropic glutamate receptors.

cards.front: Which two kinds of binding site must be filled for an NMDA receptor to open, and what fills the second kind?
cards.back: Glutamate sites and separate co-agonist sites. Glycine or D-serine fills the co-agonist sites.
cards.quote: The NMDA receptor has two kinds of binding site: glutamate sites and separate co-agonist sites.

cards.front: An NMDA receptor has glutamate and glycine bound, at normal extracellular magnesium. Compare its current with the membrane at a negative potential and after depolarization.
cards.back: Little current at negative potentials; a much larger current after depolarization.
cards.why: Magnesium ions strongly block the pore at negative membrane potentials, and depolarization relieves much of that block.
cards.quote: magnesium ions strongly block its pore at negative membrane potentials; depolarization relieves much of that block and allows a larger current

cards.front: An enzyme inhibitor prolongs acetylcholine signaling by slowing its breakdown in the cleft. Would inhibiting a cleft enzyme prolong glutamate signaling the same way?
cards.back: No. There is no glutamate-destroying enzyme in the cleft. High-affinity transporters in glia and presynaptic terminals clear glutamate, so the off switch to block would be those transporters.
cards.quote: High-affinity transporters in glia and presynaptic terminals clear it from the cleft.

cards.front: How do GABA-A and GABA-B receptors differ in receptor class?
cards.back: GABA-A receptors are ligand-gated chloride channels (ionotropic). GABA-B receptors are GPCRs (metabotropic), built from two different subunits, GB1 and GB2.
cards.quote: GABA-A receptors are ligand-gated chloride channels. GABA-B receptors are GPCRs, built from two different subunits, GB1 and GB2.

cards.front: Bicuculline and diazepam both bind GABA-A receptors. How do their binding sites and actions differ?
cards.back: Bicuculline sits in the GABA site without opening the channel: a competitive antagonist. Diazepam binds a separate site at a subunit interface and strengthens GABA's effect: a positive allosteric modulator.
cards.quote: Benzodiazepines such as diazepam are positive allosteric modulators: they bind at an interface of GABA-A subunits separate from the GABA sites.

cards.front: Strychnine is applied to the spinal cord. What happens to inhibition there, and why?
cards.back: Much of the spinal cord's inhibition is lost.
cards.why: Glycine carries much spinal inhibition through strychnine-sensitive chloride channels, and strychnine blocks these inhibitory glycine receptors.
cards.quote: Glycine carries much of the inhibition in the spinal cord, through strychnine-sensitive chloride channels.

cards.front: Among acetylcholine, dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin, which is ended mainly by an enzyme, and which enzyme?
cards.back: Acetylcholine, hydrolysed by acetylcholinesterase, most famously at the neuromuscular junction. The amines are ended by transporter uptake.
cards.quote: Acetylcholine is the one in the table ended by an enzyme: acetylcholinesterase hydrolyses it at many cholinergic synapses

cards.front: What are the major sources of brain dopamine, and what class of receptor reads it?
cards.back: The substantia nigra and ventral tegmental area of the midbrain. D1-like (D1, D5) and D2-like (D2, D3, D4) receptors, all GPCRs.
cards.quote: Substantia nigra and ventral tegmental area (midbrain)

cards.front: Which nucleus is the major source of brain noradrenaline, where is it, and what ends noradrenaline's action?
cards.back: The locus coeruleus, in the pons. Uptake by the noradrenaline transporter, NET.
cards.quote: Uptake by the noradrenaline transporter, NET

cards.front: What is the major source of brain serotonin, and what ends its action?
cards.back: The dorsal and median raphe nuclei of the brainstem. Uptake by the serotonin transporter, SERT.
cards.quote: Dorsal and median raphe nuclei (brainstem)

cards.front: Most serotonin receptors are GPCRs; the exception, the {{c1::5-HT3}} receptor, is a ligand-gated channel.
cards.quote: Note the exception among the receptors: the 5-HT3 receptor is a ligand-gated channel.

cards.front: Donepezil inhibits acetylcholinesterase. What happens to the action of each release of acetylcholine, and why?
cards.back: Each release acts for longer.
cards.why: With the enzyme slowed, acetylcholine stays in the cleft longer and keeps reaching receptors. Donepezil changes the removal step.
cards.quote: With the enzyme slowed, acetylcholine stays in the cleft longer and keeps reaching receptors, so each release acts for longer.

cards.front: How do amine transporters such as SERT move transmitter back into the terminal?
cards.back: They use the sodium gradient to carry the amine back in. SERT's uptake depends on sodium and chloride.
cards.quote: The amines are ended by transporters that use the sodium gradient to carry them back into the terminal

cards.front: A drug selectively blocks the noradrenaline transporter, NET. In prefrontal cortex, which other transmitter's signals would it be expected to prolong, and why?
cards.back: Dopamine's, because in prefrontal cortex dopamine is also taken up by NET.
cards.quote: In prefrontal cortex, dopamine is also taken up by NET.

cards.front: How are neuropeptides packaged, read and ended, compared with the amines?
cards.back: They are packaged in large dense-core vesicles and act mostly at GPCRs. Peptidases cut them into inactive fragments (some stay active), so reuptake is not their main off switch, unlike the amines.
cards.quote: Peptidases usually cut them into inactive fragments (some fragments stay active), so reuptake is not their main off switch

cards.front: In adult mouse slices, some substantia nigra dopamine neurons also release GABA onto striatal projection neurons. With all dopamine receptors blocked, would stimulating these axons still inhibit the projection neurons?
cards.back: Yes, the GABA-mediated inhibition would be expected to remain.
cards.why: "A dopamine neuron" names a cell's main transmitter, not its only one, so a drug aimed at one transmitter can leave its partner untouched.
cards.quote: a drug aimed at one transmitter of a neuron may leave its partner untouched

cards.front: In adult mouse slices, the GABA released by some substantia nigra dopamine neurons depends on uptake through the transporter Gat1. Predict how blocking Gat1 would affect the GABA these neurons release, and contrast this with the usual effect of a GAT1 blocker.
cards.back: It would be expected to reduce the GABA these neurons release, since their GABA supply depends on Gat1 uptake. In the lesson's mature postsynaptic example where GABA inhibits, a GAT1 blocker such as tiagabine instead strengthens inhibition by slowing GABA removal.
cards.why: The same transporter can serve removal in one circuit and supply in another. A drug's effect depends on which step it changes in that circuit.
cards.quote: Melani and Tritsch (2022) found that this GABA depends on uptake through the transporter Gat1

cards.front: What is a drug's dissociation constant, KD?
cards.back: The free drug concentration at which half the binding sites are filled.
cards.quote: The dissociation constant is the free drug concentration at which half the binding sites are filled.
cards.section: How much: occupancy and the factor 1 + L/K

cards.front: For one class of site at equilibrium, the fraction of targets occupied is f = {{c1::L / (KD + L)}}, where L is the free drug concentration.
cards.quote: f = L / (KD + L) Here f is the fraction of transporters occupied and L the free drug concentration.
cards.section: How much: occupancy and the factor 1 + L/K

cards.front: A drug binds its target with KD = 5 nM, assuming one class of site, equilibrium, and free drug equal to added drug. What fraction of targets is occupied at 20 nM free drug?
cards.back: f = L/(KD + L) = 20/(5 + 20) = 20/25 = 0.80, so 80% of targets are occupied.
cards.quote: Assume one class of site, equilibrium, and so little binding that free drug equals added drug.
cards.section: How much: occupancy and the factor 1 + L/K

cards.front: A drug binds its target with KD = 3 nM (one class of site, equilibrium). What free concentrations give 90% and 99% occupancy, and how many times more drug does 99% need?
cards.back: L = f × KD/(1 − f). For 90%: 0.90 × 3/0.10 = 27 nM. For 99%: 0.99 × 3/0.01 = 297 nM. That is 11 times more, all to fill the last 9% of sites.
cards.quote: That is 11 times the concentration needed for 90%, all to fill the last 9% of sites.
cards.section: How much: occupancy and the factor 1 + L/K

cards.front: Assume one class of binding site, equilibrium with fixed occupancy during clearance, occupied transporters unable to transport, and binding KD describing blockade. If a transporter is the only route out and works far below saturation, why does a blocker stretch the transmitter signal by 1 + L/KD?
cards.back: Only free transporters clear transmitter, and the free share is 1 − f = KD/(KD + L). Clearance slows by 1/(1 − f) = (KD + L)/KD = 1 + L/KD.
cards.quote: Then only the free transporters clear serotonin, and the free share is 1 − f = KD / (KD + L).
cards.section: How much: occupancy and the factor 1 + L/K

cards.front: Paroxetine binds SERT with KD = 0.08 nM. In a toy model, SERT is the only route out for serotonin, works far below saturation, and its block follows the binding KD. Free paroxetine is 0.40 nM. What share of SERT is occupied, and how many times longer does serotonin linger?
cards.quote: Uptake runs slower, and serotonin lingers longer, by the factor 1 / (1 − f) = (KD + L) / KD = 1 + L / KD
cards.section: How much: occupancy and the factor 1 + L/K

cards.front: GABA gives half-maximal current at a GABA-A receptor at 10 µM (its EC50). A competitive antagonist with KB = 0.5 µM is present at 2 µM. What is the dose ratio, what is GABA's apparent EC50, and what happens to the maximum current?
cards.back: Dose ratio = 1 + [B]/KB = 1 + 2/0.5 = 5. Apparent EC50 = 5 × 10 µM = 50 µM. The maximum is unchanged: enough GABA still fills the sites.
cards.quote: The antagonist makes each GABA site 1 + [B]/KB times harder to fill, so GABA must be that many times more concentrated
cards.section: How much: occupancy and the factor 1 + L/K

cards.front: An agonist's EC50 at a receptor is 5 µM. With a competitive antagonist at 2 µM, the curve shifts right in parallel with the same maximum, and the EC50 becomes 25 µM. Estimate the antagonist's KB.
cards.back: Dose ratio = 25/5 = 5 = 1 + [B]/KB, so [B]/KB = 4 and KB = 2 µM/4 = 0.5 µM.
cards.quote: dose ratio = 1 + [B] / KB = 1 + 3/1 = 4
cards.section: How much: occupancy and the factor 1 + L/K

cards.front: On a plot of GABA-A current against log GABA concentration, how do bicuculline and diazepam change the curve?
cards.back: Bicuculline slides it to the right, with the same maximum. Diazepam slides it to the left, and opens few or no channels by itself.
cards.quote: With bicuculline, the same curve slides to the right and still reaches the same top. With diazepam, it slides to the left.
cards.section: How much: occupancy and the factor 1 + L/K

cards.front: Ever higher concentrations of a competitive antagonist are added to a receptor, and in a separate experiment ever higher concentrations of a positive allosteric modulator. How far does each keep shifting the agonist's dose-response curve?
cards.back: The competitive antagonist keeps shifting it right, by 1 + [B]/KB, for as long as more is added. The modulator's shift stops once its own sites are full.
cards.why: A positive allosteric modulator has a ceiling set by its own saturation; a competitor has none.
cards.quote: a positive allosteric modulator has a ceiling set by its own saturation
cards.section: How much: occupancy and the factor 1 + L/K

cards.front: Under what conditions does the factor 1 + L/K describe a drug's effect?
cards.back: For the immediate action, at one target and at equilibrium, of a drug that competes for the natural molecule's site: a competitive antagonist at a receptor (1 + L/K is the dose ratio), or a competitive inhibitor at a transporter or enzyme. It means slowed uptake only if the carrier works far below saturation, and a stretched whole signal only if the blocked route is the only way out and occupancy stays fixed; occupied transporters cannot transport and the binding KD is assumed to describe blockade.
cards.quote: It describes the immediate action of a drug at one target, at equilibrium, when the drug competes for the natural molecule's site
cards.section: How much: occupancy and the factor 1 + L/K

cards.front: In a toy model, paroxetine's occupancy of SERT gives a stretch factor 1 + L/KD = 10. Can that number predict how much a patient's synaptic serotonin changes after weeks of treatment, or how much the drug helps? Why not?
cards.back: No. The factor gives only the immediate effect at one target at equilibrium, from SERT in cell membranes. It does not predict chronic adaptation, other clearance routes or clinical benefit.
cards.why: Rests on the stated scope of 1 + L/K: a model number, not a measured synaptic change or a dose for a person.
cards.quote: they are not a measured change in synaptic serotonin and not a dose for a person
cards.section: How much: occupancy and the factor 1 + L/K

cards.front: Delgado and colleagues (1990) gave 21 patients whose depression had remitted on antidepressants a tryptophan-free amino-acid challenge and a control challenge, double-blind and in crossover. Fourteen relapsed after tryptophan depletion; the control had no significant effect. What does this show, and why does it not show that low serotonin causes depression?
cards.back: It suggests that remission in some treated patients depends on serotonin being available. The patients were chosen because they had responded to antidepressants, and a treatment can depend on a transmitter that was never low.
cards.quote: The result suggests that remission in some treated patients depends on serotonin being available.

cards.front: Design a tryptophan-depletion study that tests whether low serotonin causes depression, rather than whether treatment depends on serotonin.
cards.back: Study people not on antidepressants: never-depressed people and untreated people with depression, analysed separately. Give tryptophan depletion and a balanced control drink containing tryptophan, double-blind and in crossover. Check that blood tryptophan fell, compare mood during depletion with the control session in each group over the hours observed, and report how many participants changed, not only group means. This tests whether an acute fall in serotonin synthesis is sufficient to lower mood; a null result does not rule out a chronic or vulnerability-dependent role.
cards.quote: To test whether low serotonin causes depression, you would study people who are not on these drugs.

cards.front: SSRIs block SERT and help many people with depression. Does that show depression is caused by low serotonin?
cards.back: No. That SSRIs block SERT is an established mechanism; that low serotonin causes depression is a separate claim. Aspirin relieves headaches, but headaches are not caused by a lack of aspirin.
cards.quote: Aspirin relieves a headache, and headaches are not caused by a lack of aspirin.

cards.front: A drug shifts an agonist's dose-response curve to the right at one concentration. How can you tell whether it is a competitive antagonist or a negative allosteric modulator?
cards.back: Test several concentrations. For a competitor at equilibrium, the dose ratio minus 1 grows in direct proportion to its concentration (the Schild relation); in the lesson's affinity-only negative allosteric model, the shift levels off as its own sites fill. These patterns help distinguish them, and binding or structural experiments add evidence on where the drug sits.
cards.quote: One concentration cannot tell the two apart. Several can help, and binding or structural experiments add evidence on where the drug sits.
cards.section: Telling a competitor from a modulator

cards.front: In a well-mixed model with fixed parallel first-order clearance, drug-insensitive routes supply 10% of serotonin's baseline clearance rate constant and the transporter 90%. A blocker fills 90% of the transporters. How much longer is serotonin's decay time constant, and what is the most any dose could give?
cards.back: Remaining clearance = 0.90 × 0.10 + 0.10 = 0.19 of baseline, so the time constant lengthens 1/0.19 ≈ 5.3-fold, not 10-fold. With full block the limit is 1/0.10 = 10-fold.
cards.quote: Then blocking the transporter can lengthen serotonin's decay time constant at most 1/0.05 = 20-fold, however much drug you add
cards.section: Where the factor 1 + L/K stops working

cards.front: Serotonin opened single channels in outside-out patches excised from guinea-pig enteric neurons. Why did this show that the 5-HT3 receptor is a ligand-gated channel?
cards.back: An excised patch lacks the cell's cytoplasm, so no messenger chain inside the cell could carry the signal. The receptor itself had to be the channel.
cards.quote: A response in an excised patch, without the cell's cytoplasm, showed that the 5-HT3 receptor is a ligand-gated channel.
cards.section: How the 5-HT3 receptor was shown to be a channel

cards.front: Conclusion: in cultured mouse brain neurons, glycine potentiates NMDA receptor responses by a mechanism separate from the inhibitory glycine receptor. What result with strychnine supports this, and why?
cards.back: The potentiation persists when strychnine blocks the inhibitory glycine receptors, which supports a separate mechanism. Glycine is separately known as an NMDA co-agonist, but strychnine resistance alone does not establish the exact binding site.
cards.quote: glycine potentiated NMDA receptor responses by a mechanism separate from the inhibitory glycine receptor
